BERT4Rec requires masked-target training and next-item inference from an appended mask token. For this task’s left-padded histories, read the final nonpadding position—the appended mask—never count−1; keep targets outside bidirectional inputs. Apply identical truncation, padding and mask placement to every intervention. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690).

Recent work supports history interventions but cautions against equating prediction changes with explanation quality. A 2025 sequential-counterfactual study searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations. RecSys 2025’s Beyond Top-1 finds explanation metrics depend on recommender quality and investigates evaluating multiple recommended items rather than only the first. Neither establishes that sensitivity proves correct use of recent history. [Sequential counterfactuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606), [Beyond Top-1](https://evazangerle.at/publication/mohammadi-recsys-2025/mohammadi-recsys-2025.pdf).

Practical synthesis, proposed rather than a published BERT4Rec protocol: delete the last k interactions versus equally sized random and older-history deletions; permute a recent window while preserving its item multiset; replace selected items using controls matched on training frequency and title/description similarity. Deletion also changes sequence length and positions, so interpret it alongside length-preserving permutations and replacements. Freeze candidate sets and eligibility masks across interventions. Measure signed target-score changes, target-rank changes, top-10 overlap and paired validation HR@10 changes. Repeat random controls and bootstrap users within each category for confidence intervals on intervention-minus-control effects and their macro-average. Report baseline-correct and baseline-incorrect cases separately: recommendation instability measures dependence; worsening held-out validation ranks provides evidence that the dependence was useful. Keep one fixed trained checkpoint per category throughout these probes.
